newsitem.title: BELGIUM: Belgian budget to contain debt reduction measures.
newsitem.headline: Belgian budget to contain debt reduction measures.

text.p: Belgium's 1997 budget will likely contain big measures to cut the country's debt to gross domestic product (GDP) ratio, aimed to help it qualify for the European economic and monetary union, officials said on Friday.

"The effort will be (to cut the ratio by) between three and four percentage points in 1997," one official said. Another said the target was part of an objective to make sure the debt to GDP ratio, the highest in Europe, decreased by 10 percentage points between 1993 and 1997.
Belgium's debt was 137.9 percent of GDP at the end of 1993 and is forecast to fall to 131.8 percent of GDP by the end of 1996, according to the country's 1996 budget.

Debt is Belgium's biggest hurdle in its bid to qualify for EMU, due to start in 1999. The Maastricht Treaty says that countries who want to join must cut their debt to 60 percent of GDP or be approaching that level at a "satisfactory pace".
Belgium already meets other criteria outlined in the Treaty on inflation, long-term interest rates and currency stability within Europe's exchange rate mechanism (ERM).
The government is also seen drawing up austerity measures estimated at around 100 billion Belgian francs to ensure its deficitto GDP ratio also meets the three percent requirement.
The budget must be finished by October 1.
But cutting the debt will require a further exceptional effort, probably from government asset sales, including property, one official said.

Belgium's local authorities may be asked to acquire central government debt through the profit raised from the sale this autumn of around 30 percent of municipally owned Credit Communal /Gemeentekrediet, Belgium's second largest bank.
Under Maastricht calculations, debt held by local authorities would not be taken into consideration when calculating Belgium's gross debt, one official said.
More controversially, the government could revive a four year old proposal to use the surplus on the Belgian National Bank's gold reserves to back a fund to cut the debt, informed sources said.
Belgium currently has 236 billion francs in the BNB's balance sheet that represents the difference in the price the central bank paid to acquire its gold and its market value.
The surplus is held in the form of foreign exchange reserves on which the government earns interest income.

Four years ago Belgian Senator Etienne Cooreman, who is currently also chairman of the Brussels Stock Exchange, proposed using the reserve to create a fund to gradually acquire and repay government debt. One source said this idea still has some support in government circles.
However, use of the gold reserve to cut the debt would require a change in the Belgian National Bank's statutes, another source said.
He noted that by removing the gold reserve from the bank's balance sheet the government would also lose the interest it presently earns, making the benefit of such a move unclear.
